items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.quote: the controller must ensure that safeguards for the data subject’s rights, freedoms and legitimate interests are in place
items.why: The binding rule. The duty sits on the controller and is to ensure the safeguards 'are in place', which is the legal root of the question whether they really work. Four measures: information about the decision, representations, human intervention on the part of the controller, contest. Applies only to a significant decision based on personal data and based solely on automated processing. Substituted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80(1); fully in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82). Article 22D(3), read alongside, lets ministers add to or specify the safeguards by regulations; the annotations show none.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 24: Responsibility of the controller
items.quote: to ensure and to be able to demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with this Regulation
items.why: Why evidence matters. The controller must implement technical and organisational measures both to comply and to be able to show it, and must review and update them. This reaches Article 22C directly; Article 5(2), also read, attaches the duty to demonstrate only to the principles in Article 5(1).

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 83: General conditions for imposing administrative fines
items.locator: Art. 83(5), point (ba); notes F8 and F10
items.quote: Article 22B or 22C (restrictions on, and safeguards for, automated decision-making)
items.why: Source of the figure. Point (ba), inserted 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 Sch. 6 para. 9(b), names Article 22B and 22C in the higher tier: up to £17,500,000 or, for an undertaking, 4% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. The page prints the percentage as '4 %'. The text reads 'the Commission' from 30 September 2026. Data Protection Act 2018 s.157(5), read alongside, gives the same amounts.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 146: Assessment notices
items.quote: carry out an assessment of whether the controller or processor has complied or is complying with the data protection legislation
items.why: How a paper safeguard would be found out. The regulator may require access to premises, documents, equipment and staff for interview, may observe processing, and (since 2026) may require a report from an approved person. Sections 149 and 155, read alongside, allow an enforcement notice or a penalty notice for failing to comply with Articles 12 to 22D. Text reads 'the Commission'; amended 5 February and 30 September 2026.

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What are the ADM safeguards? (draft guidance for consultation)
items.locator: Sections 'What are the safeguards in the ADM provisions?', 'What is human intervention?' and 'How do we enable people to contest decisions?'
items.quote: You must apply the safeguards consistently rather than on an ad hoc discretionary basis.
items.why: The regulator's reading of Article 22C from the organisation's side. Consultation draft dated 31 March 2026 (consultation closed 29 May 2026); not final and may change. Asks for a system that delivers an audit trail, a record of how the human reviewed the decision, trained reviewers with authority to alter the decision, monitoring and analysis of review outcomes, and 'measures in place' to challenge or appeal. The word 'operational' does not appear.

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What else do we need to consider? (draft guidance for consultation)
items.locator: Sections 'Do we have to do a data protection impact assessment (DPIA)?' and 'Do we need to make any other changes to our systems?', final paragraph
items.quote: monitoring aspects of a system’s performance, such as its statistical accuracy, is not human intervention
items.why: Draws the line between testing the system and running the safeguard: quality checks on a sample of decisions and audits of the model are expected, but they do not count as human intervention. Also says the impact assessment must include processes that ensure people receive information about the processing and their rights. Consultation draft; not final.

items.title: Recruitment rewired: Transparency and safeguards
items.locator: Section 'Our findings about transparency and safeguards', sub-section 'Safeguards', including the third case study (chatbot screening interviews), and 'Expectations'
items.quote: We also didn’t see widespread evidence that candidates were able to make representations, obtain human intervention or contest decisions.
items.why: Source of the quotation and the only UK evidence found on whether safeguards exist in practice. Includes the employer that told candidates of the right to human intervention but had no method for handling requests, and the regulator's expectation of 'clear processes set up to handle these requests promptly'. Limits: recruitment only; voluntary engagement with over 30 employers, not an audit; mostly gathered before Articles 22A-22D were in force. No date is printed on the page; page metadata gives 31 March 2026.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Accountability toolkit: Information rights
items.locator: Final control measure but one: 'People’s rights related to automated decision-making and profiling are protected'; also the control measures on resources, logging and monitoring of requests
items.quote: ensure a recorded process allows simple ways for people to request human intervention, express their opinion and challenge a decision
items.why: What the regulator's auditors look for: a recorded process, a specific person or team responsible for requests, a log showing due date, response date and action taken, reports on performance to senior management, and a check on whether a sample of requests followed the procedure. The nearest source for the word 'operational' ('adequate operational procedures in place'). Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; still refers to Article 22. No date printed; page metadata gives 20 November 2024.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Artificial intelligence toolkit: Human review
items.locator: First control measure, 'Ways to meet our expectations'; second control measure, 'Ways to meet our expectations' and 'Options to consider'
items.quote: Maintain a log of when AI decisions are overridden by a human reviewer, including the reasons why.
items.why: Evidence and testing for the human intervention safeguard: a documented test plan, an override log with reasons, results reported to senior management, reviewers with a manageable caseload, training and independence, and the process tested on a sample of decisions. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; still refers to Article 22. No date printed; page metadata gives 20 November 2024.

items.title: Guidelines on Automated individual decision-making and Profiling for the purposes of Regulation 2016/679 (WP251rev.01)
items.publisher: Article 29 Data Protection Working Party (endorsed by the European Data Protection Board, 25 May 2018)
items.locator: Chapter IV, section F 'Establishing appropriate safeguards', p.27; Annex 1 good practice recommendations, row 'Appropriate safeguards', p.32
items.quote: The controller must provide a simple way for the data subject to exercise these rights.
items.why: European comparator, on Article 22 of the EU GDPR (the text the UK replaced). Suggests an appeals link at the point the decision is delivered, agreed timescales for the review, a named contact point, and regular quality assurance and algorithmic auditing whose results feed back into system design. PDF served from the European Commission's Article 29 archive. Not UK guidance and not binding in the UK.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 50C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.quote: the controller reconsiders the decision as soon as reasonably practicable
items.why: The law enforcement counterpart of UK GDPR Article 22C: the same four safeguards, with one exemption that itself requires a working process, namely prompt reconsideration with meaningful human involvement. Shows that even where the safeguards are disapplied the statute expects an operating review route. Limits: applies only to competent authorities under Part 3. Substituted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80(3), fully in force 5 February 2026.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies
items.locator: Section on completing Tier 2, 'What information is relevant for the appeals and review field?'
items.quote: You should consider both the outputs of the algorithmic tool itself and whether they can be challenged or appealed
items.why: The government standard requires each published record to say how a tool's outputs, and the wider process, can be challenged or appealed, with a link to the route. A public, checkable statement of the contest safeguard per system. Limits: government policy, not statute; mandatory only for central government bodies in scope; the passage still quotes the old Article 22, not Articles 22A to 22D. Used by other briefs for different passages.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 3, MEASURE 3.3 (p. 30); see also Table 4, MANAGE 4.1 (p. 32)
items.quote: Feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes are established and integrated into AI system evaluation metrics.
items.why: International comparator. The nearest published standard to the criterion's upper levels: appeal routes are not only to exist but to be measured and fed into how the system is evaluated. MANAGE 4.1 adds 'appeal and override' to post-deployment monitoring plans. Limits: voluntary United States framework, not UK law; it does not set out the four UK statutory safeguards.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 86: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken
items.why: A separate EU safeguard that reaches UK firms deploying high-risk systems in the EU: a person significantly affected by a decision based on such a system can demand an explanation from the deployer. It applies whether or not a human was involved, so it is wider than the UK 'solely automated' trigger. Limits: this is the Commission's copy, stated to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026; the article carries no NEW or AMENDED marker; no application date is taken from it. Not UK law.

items.title: Ensuring statistical models command public confidence: learning lessons from the approach to developing models for awarding grades in the UK in 2020
items.locator: Executive summary, findings on quality assurance and on meeting the need; the full report is a download from the same page
items.quote: There was limited human review of outputs of the models at an individual level prior to results day.
items.why: Official review of the 2020 exam grading models. The regulators relied on an appeals process to catch individual errors in place of human review before results were issued; the review found the limits of the models and the role of appeals were not well communicated, and recommends being clear on the timing and grounds for appeal. A UK case of a safeguard that existed on paper and did not hold. Limits: a statistics regulator's review against the Code of Practice for Statistics; it expressly does not judge compliance with data protection law.

items.title: The Right to Contest AI
items.publisher: Margot E. Kaminski and Jennifer M. Urban, Columbia Law Review vol. 121 no. 7
items.locator: Abstract and Introduction on the journal's own page
items.quote: This Article establishes four contestation archetypes that should serve as the bases of discussions of contestation
items.why: The fullest academic treatment found of what a working right to contest needs. It sorts contest schemes by whether they rest on rules or standards and on procedure or substantive rights, and examines the European right in depth. Useful for judging whether a contest route is real. Limits: a United States law review article (student-edited, not peer reviewed in the scientific sense), written for a US audience before the UK's 2025 changes; argument, not measurement.

items.title: Conceptualising Contestability: Perspectives on Contesting Algorithmic Decisions
items.publisher: Henrietta Lyons, Eduardo Velloso and Tim Miller, Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW), authors' copy on arXiv
items.quote: while the nature of contestability is disputed, it is seen as a way to protect individuals
items.why: Peer-reviewed analysis of submissions to Australia's proposed AI ethics framework. Finds little agreement on what contestability requires in practice, and that respondents model it on how human decisions are challenged. Supports the point that naming a right does not specify a process. Limits: Australian policy submissions, qualitative; only the abstract is on the linked page; no evidence on how often safeguards are used or how well they work.
